title: Transformer — 7 Learning Questions
subtitle: Topic: Transformer Architecture and Attention Mechanisms · Subject: Transformers and LLM Architecture. Seven questions, four balanced options each, and seven distinct technical diagrams.
hero:
TRANSFORMER · ILLUSTRATED OVERVIEW

Words become vectors. Attention connects their meaning.

A Transformer models token relationships through attention and learned layers, enabling language understanding and sequence generation.

questions.stem: What is a Transformer in Artificial Intelligence, and how does it process and understand sequences of information such as text?
options: It carries information forward through a hidden state, processing each token after the previous token. That describes recurrent networks rather than a Transformer using attention across positions.
It uses attention to connect relevant tokens in a sequence, letting each token learn from other positions while the model builds useful context for its predictions.
It searches a collection of saved sentences and returns the closest stored response. That describes retrieval rather than neural attention learning the relationships between tokens in context.
It gives every token a position number and tries to understand meaning from those numbers alone. Position information helps, but it cannot replace learning relationships between words.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine reading a mystery in which a detective says, “The key was under the vase. It was missing yesterday.” To understand “it,” you look back at the key. A Transformer does something similar using attention: a token can use information from other relevant tokens. Attention helps the model build useful representations for tasks such as translation and question answering. Position information also helps it understand order. Remember: attention connects related information across a sequence; it does not simply read one word at a time.
questions.figure:
01 · CORE IDEA

How one token can combine context from a whole sentence

Attention gives each position a way to use relevant tokens; positional information helps the network distinguish sequence order.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. The Transformer processes token representations with attention. This lets different positions gather information from other relevant positions, while positional information helps distinguish sequence order. Transformer architectures support classification, translation and text generation.

questions.stem: Why was the Transformer architecture introduced, and what limitations of earlier sequence models such as Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks was it designed to overcome?
options: It mostly solves the problem of splitting sentences into tokens before learning begins. Tokenization prepares input text, but it does not remove the step-by-step processing of RNNs.
It removes all learned weights from language models so they can predict words faster. Transformer attention still needs carefully trained parameters to recognize useful relationships between tokens.
It gives recurrent hidden states more space to remember earlier words, while still passing memory from one step to the next. That helps RNNs but preserves sequential processing.
It processes many input positions together with attention during training, reducing the sequential bottleneck of RNNs while helping distant words share useful information across a sentence.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture a long shipping manifest with hundreds of entries. An RNN typically handles entries in order, passing a hidden state to the next step. That makes training harder to parallelize, and early details can become difficult to retain. A Transformer uses attention to compare many input positions together during training, so it can connect a package number near the beginning with its destination far later. It still needs computation and memory, but it removes much of the sequential bottleneck.
questions.figure:
02 · WHY TRANSFORMERS

Compare chained recurrence with parallel attention

LSTMs improve memory of earlier signals, but their recurrence still links computations across timesteps. Transformers allow parallel training across sequence positions.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. RNNs and LSTMs recurrently process positions in order, which limits training parallelization and can make long-distance dependencies difficult. Transformers use attention to connect distant positions directly and process sequence positions more in parallel.

questions.stem: How does a Transformer process an input sentence step by step, from tokenization and input embeddings to positional information, attention mechanisms, and generating output predictions?
options: It splits text into tokens, turns them into vectors, adds position information, applies attention and other learned layers, and then generates predictions from the resulting representations.
It turns sentences into final probabilities before splitting them into tokens. Softmax can produce probabilities, but it cannot replace the input tokenization and embedding steps of a Transformer.
It begins with position numbers instead of word embeddings and learns meaning from those numbers alone. Positions tell the model order but not the content of its words.
It produces the complete answer before processing the input, then uses attention to confirm its guess. Transformers must first build input representations to make informed predictions.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose the input is “Reserve two seats.” A tokenizer breaks it into tokens, and embeddings turn them into vectors. Position information tells the model their order. Attention helps connect “two” with “seats,” while more layers refine the representation. Finally, an output layer produces predictions, such as a next token or a task label. The path is tokens → embeddings and positions → attention and processing → output. The exact result depends on what the model was built to do.
questions.figure:
03 · INPUT TO OUTPUT

Follow tokens through five different computations

Actual Transformer stacks repeat attention and feed-forward layers. Depending on the task, final predictions may represent tokens, classes, or an output sequence.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Text is tokenized into token IDs, embedded into vectors, and enriched with position information. Attention and feed-forward blocks form contextual representations. A final output head then produces token or task-specific predictions.

questions.stem: How does the original Transformer architecture work internally, including encoder and decoder blocks, Query (Q), Key (K), Value (V) matrices, scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, feed-forward networks, residual connections, layer normalization, and attention masking?
options: An encoder creates the final answer and sends it backward through a decoder to discover important source-language relationships. In the original design, the encoder builds input representations first.
A decoder looks at future output words freely during next-token generation, so it can avoid wrong predictions. Causal masking actually blocks those future output positions.
Attention uses queries to match keys and combine values. Multiple heads learn different links; feed-forward layers, residual paths, and normalization help the model process information.
Queries, keys, and values are produced after Softmax chooses the output words. In attention, these projections are made before attention scores are normalized and combined.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Think of translating a train-station announcement. The encoder reads source words and builds representations. The decoder generates an output using earlier output words and, through cross-attention, information from the encoder. Query, Key, and Value vectors help attention select relevant information. Multiple heads can learn different relationships. Feed-forward layers transform the results, and residual connections and normalization support deep processing. Masks stop the decoder from looking at output words it has not generated yet.
questions.figure:
04 · ORIGINAL TRANSFORMER

Trace encoder memory, decoder masking, Q/K/V and cross-attention

In the original 2017 Transformer, positional encodings enter the stacks, residual-plus-normalization wraps each sublayer, and the decoder's self-attention is causally masked.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: C. The 2017 Transformer combines encoder self-attention with feed-forward layers and decoder masked self-attention, encoder-decoder cross-attention and feed-forward layers. Each attention head projects Q/K/V and applies scaled dot-product attention. Residual connections, layer normalization, positional encoding and attention masks are fundamental components.

questions.stem: How can a simplified Transformer be implemented from scratch using Python and PyTorch, including token embeddings, positional encoding, multi-head self-attention, feed-forward layers, attention masks, and a basic training loop?
options: Build a recurrent loop that reads tokens in order and trains only its hidden state. That can make an RNN, but it leaves out Transformer attention mechanisms.
Create token embeddings and position information, apply multi-head attention and masks, add feed-forward layers, then train the model with a loss function and optimizer.
Map each token directly to a class label and use those labels as the complete network. That skips the contextual representations learned by a Transformer attention block.
Train only a position table and freeze it before building the rest of the network. Position values alone cannot teach a model relationships between word meanings.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine building a tiny model that completes short calendar reminders. In PyTorch, begin with token IDs and an embedding layer. Add position information, an attention block, and a feed-forward block. For next-token prediction, apply a causal mask so the model cannot see future tokens. The network produces scores for possible next tokens. A loss function compares them with the correct next token, and an optimizer updates weights. Start small enough to inspect each stage of the training loop.
questions.figure:
05 · PYTORCH WALKTHROUGH

Read the manual attention implementation next to a tensor-flow map

● ● ● tiny_transformer.py · executable PyTorch
import torch
from torch import nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TinyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab=32, d=32, h=4):
        super().__init__()
        self.d, self.h = d, h
        self.embed = nn.Embedding(vocab, d)
        self.pos = nn.Embedding(64, d)
        self.qkv = nn.Linear(d, 3*d)
        self.proj = nn.Linear(d, d)
        self.ff = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 4*d),
                                nn.GELU(), nn.Linear(4*d, d))
        self.ln1, self.ln2 = nn.LayerNorm(d), nn.LayerNorm(d)
        self.readout = nn.Linear(d, vocab)

    def forward(self, ids):
        b, t = ids.shape
        x = self.embed(ids) + self.pos(
            torch.arange(t, device=ids.device))
        q, k, v = self.qkv(x).reshape(
            b, t, 3, self.h, self.d//self.h
        ).permute(2, 0, 3, 1, 4)
        scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)
        scores = scores / (self.d//self.h)**0.5
        future = torch.ones(t, t, device=ids.device,
            dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
        weights = scores.masked_fill(
            future, -torch.inf).softmax(-1)
        a = (weights @ v).transpose(1, 2)
        a = a.reshape(b, t, self.d)
        x = self.ln1(x + self.proj(a))
        x = self.ln2(x + self.ff(x))
        return self.readout(x)

model = TinyTransformer()
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
tokens = torch.randint(0, 32, (4, 9))
for _ in range(3):  # Toy demonstration data
    x, y = tokens[:, :-1], tokens[:, 1:]
    logits = model(x)
    loss = F.cross_entropy(
        logits.reshape(-1, 32), y.reshape(-1))
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
print(f"Loss: {loss.item():.3f}")

The example uses random tokens only to demonstrate a real forward/backward pass, not language proficiency.

Q/K/V are computed explicitly, split across heads, masked before Softmax, then combined with residual and feed-forward layers. The short loop trains on next-token cross entropy.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: B. A basic PyTorch model embeds tokens, adds positions, computes Q/K/V projections and splits attention into heads. It applies a causal mask before Softmax, merges head outputs and uses residual, normalization and feed-forward layers. Next-token cross-entropy drives parameter updates. The code shown uses demonstration tokens only.

questions.stem: How do encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder Transformer architectures differ, and how do models such as BERT, GPT, and T5 use bidirectional attention, causal attention, cross-attention, and different training objectives for language understanding and generation?
options: BERT can only use earlier words for understanding, while GPT looks at future words when generating text. Their typical attention directions are actually the other way around.
T5 processes its input only through the decoder and never produces encoder representations. Its encoder is important because the decoder can attend to source information.
All three families use identical attention masks and training objectives, so they can be exchanged without changing a task. Their visibility rules and learning goals differ.
BERT uses bidirectional encoder attention, GPT predicts tokens using causal decoder attention, and T5 combines an encoder with a decoder to transform input text into output.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Imagine three jobs: judging the sentiment of a product review, continuing a fantasy story, and translating a road sign. A BERT-style encoder can use words on both sides to understand the review. A GPT-style decoder predicts the next token without seeing future tokens. A T5-style encoder-decoder reads the sign as input and produces translated text. All three use Transformers, but their attention patterns and training objectives differ. Choose a model family based on the job.
questions.figure:
06 · THREE ARCHITECTURES

Compare bidirectional, causal and encoder–decoder attention

BERT typically learns masked-token representations, GPT learns autoregressive predictions, and T5 trains text-to-text objectives with cross-attention.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: D. BERT uses bidirectional encoder attention and masked-language pretraining. GPT uses causal decoder attention and autoregressive next-token objectives. T5 uses encoder-decoder blocks with cross-attention and a text-to-text objective, including span-corruption pretraining.

questions.stem: What challenges arise when scaling Transformers to Large Language Models (LLMs), including quadratic attention complexity, long-context processing, KV-cache memory consumption, training instability, and inference latency, and how do techniques such as FlashAttention, Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE), sparse attention, and distributed training address these challenges?
options: FlashAttention reduces attention memory traffic, grouped-query attention shares key/value heads, and distributed training divides work across hardware to manage the growing cost of large models.
Rotary positions remove all attention calculations and replace them with numbered token labels. RoPE carries useful position information, but attention still needs scores and values.
Longer contexts make dense attention cheaper because every new token reuses all earlier computations without memory cost. In practice, more tokens usually increase attention work and caching demands.
Distributing an LLM over more GPUs removes response delays completely, even when the KV cache grows. Communication between devices and memory use can still limit speed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Picture an LLM reviewing a very long legal-hearing transcript. As tokens increase, attention can require much more work, and the KV cache consumes memory during generation. FlashAttention processes attention in tiles to reduce memory movement. Grouped-query attention stores fewer distinct key/value heads. RoPE adds position information, while distributed training shares computation across hardware. Sparse attention can skip selected connections. Each tool solves a different scaling problem; none makes long-context processing free.
questions.figure:
07 · PRODUCTION LLM BOTTLENECKS

See where memory grows and how optimization techniques respond

FlashAttention cuts attention memory I/O; GQA shrinks K/V caches; RoPE supplies relative position behavior; sparse attention changes connectivity; distributed training splits work. The trade-offs depend on workload.
questions.technicalExplanation: Correct: A. Dense self-attention has quadratic interactions in sequence length. FlashAttention optimizes exact attention with tiling, GQA reduces key/value head counts and KV-cache size, RoPE encodes positions through rotations, sparse patterns limit attended links and distributed training splits work across devices. None individually fixes every cost or stability issue.
